name: Ali Riza Göktan
train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections. This case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section of the Court. The Court ruled that the application was partly admissible and the Government filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The case was then referred to the European Court of Human rights (ECH) for further proceedings. The application was rejected.

The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) on 11 March 1996. The applicant alleged a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention and of Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. On 1 November 2001 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1) and this case was assigned to the newly composed Second Section. The Government, but not the applicant, filed written observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The Court ruled that the application was partly admissible on 27 November 2001.

The case originated in an application (no. 33402/96) against the French Republic lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human rights and Fundamental Freedoms. Mr Ali Riza Göktan (‘the applicant’), on 11 March 1996, alleged a violation of Article 6 of the Convention and of Article 4 of Protocol No. 11. The applicant was represented before the Court by Ms M.-C. Reminiac, of the Bourg-en-Bresse Bar, and Mr T. Beygo of the Istanbul Bar.

The applicant was charged with drug trafficking and sentenced to five years' imprisonment. He said he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. The couple who had "escaped" arrest by the police were in fact both customs officers, known as ‘Maud’ and ‘Serge’ The case was struck out after the applicant decided to appeal to the Court of Cassation; however, he later withdrew his appeal and the case was thrown out. The applicant is currently living in Turkey. The case took place in March 1991 in the city of Strasbourg. The application was brought by the Strasbourg Regional Police Department (“the SRPJ”)

The applicant was born in 1953 and currently lives in Turkey. He entered France in 1974. At the material time, he worked for a business in Strasbourg. He and another person, M. B., were arrested by officers from the Strasbourg Regional Police Department (“the SRPJ”) and customs officers on the verge of concluding a drugs deal with a couple. The applicant consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs. He later withdrew his appeal and the case was struck out.

B., were arrested by officers from the Strasbourg Regional Police Department (“the SRPJ”) and customs officers on the verge of concluding a drugs deal with a couple, who managed to make their getaway. The applicant consistently protested his innocence, saying that he had been the victim of a put-up job by customs officers. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment for the criminal offences of importing, purchasing, possessing and transporting drugs.

The applicant completed his prison sentence on 4 September 1994. However, he remained in custody pursuant to the order requiring him to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment of the customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the order was defective. The Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. He relied in particular on the Court's judgment in Jamil v France (judgment of 8 June 1995, Series A no. 317-B)

The applicant was ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment of a customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He made an urgent application to the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance, arguing that the order for his imprisonment was defective, as the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. The urgent-applications judge dismissed that application in an order of 27 September 1994. On 26 October 1994 the Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit.

He was sentenced to two years' imprisonment in default of payment of a customs fine of FRF 1,470,000. He appealed the order, arguing that the Customs Office had failed to serve him with a demand for payment. The appeal was dismissed by the President of the Mulhouse tribunal de grande instance. The Court of Cassation ruled that the applicant's appeal on points of law against that decision had lapsed, as he had not lodged written pleadings in support of his appeal within the statutory time-limit. The courts have consistently held that customs law is a special branch of law and an exception to the general law.

Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. After being ordered to serve two years' imprisonment in default of payment, he made an application for a ruling that that term should run concurrently with the prison sentence. The Court of Cassation dismissed the appeal for the following reasons: “The appellant cannot validly argue that, by sitting in private in accordance with Article 711 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the Court of Appeal infringed Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights’” The applicant has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

Ali Göktan was found guilty of an offence under the drug-trafficking and customs-offences legislation. He was sentenced to five years' imprisonment and a customs fine. The Court of Appeal dismissed that application on the grounds that ‘imprisonment in default possesses the legal characteristics not of a penalty, but of a means of enforcement attached to the financial penalties whose recovery they are intended to secure’ The applicant, who has now completed all the sentences he was required to serve, was deported to Turkey, where he came from, pursuant to the permanent exclusion order.

The Turkish Government (“the Government”) did not designate an Agent for the purposes of the proceedings before the Court. The applicant claims to have been insulted and beaten, in particular, hit with truncheons on the legs, and that one of the policemen sexually harassed her. The same police officer punched the applicant in her right eye after she had been placed in the police vehicle. The Court decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant, along with seventy other persons, appeared before the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance. They were charged with taking part in an unauthorised demonstration. The applicant reiterated that she had been beaten and sexually harassed during her arrest. She gave a description of the events with details about the perpetrators. On 30 January 2001 the public prosecutor decided not to prosecute the police officers who had been on duty at the relevant time. In this connection, he maintained that the complainants had taken part in a demonstration against F-type prisons. Although before intervening and making arrests the police had given the demonstrators a warning and had ordered them to disperse, the demonstrators had resisted the police and thrown stones at them. The Ministry of the Interior lodged an action for compensation against the applicant and the other co-accused and requested the reimbursement of the amount of compensation paid to the injured police officers. The court's reasoned decision refers to evidence such as eye-witness reports, video recordings of the Security Directorate and other national television channels. According to the information available in the file, the compensation proceedings were apparently still pending on the date on which the present judgment was adopted. On 22 January 2004 the Ankara Criminal Court of First Instance acquitted the applicant on account of lack of evidence. The case has been referred to the closest assize court, against the decision of 30 January 2001.

The applicant was taken into custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK (the Kurdistan Workers’ Party) In her police statements dated 6 and 8 October 1996 respectively, the applicant accepted the charges against her. She was interrogated in the absence of a lawyer by the public prosecutor and the investigating judge respectively and denied the allegations. In June 1999 the Diyarbakır State Security Court concluded that the applicant was a member of the PKK and accordingly sentenced her to eight years and four months’ imprisonment. The Court of Cassation quashed the judgment of the first-instance court on 20 December 1999. The applicant was released pending trial.

The case was settled in court in November 2002.

eval_texts: The case was referred to the Court by the European Commission of Human Rights (‘the Commission’) on 1 September 1992, within the three-month period laid down by Article 32 para. 1 and Article 47 (art. 32-1, art. 47) of the Convention. It originated in an application (no. 12235/86) against the Republic of Austria lodged with the Commission under Article 25. The object of the request was to obtain a decision as to whether the facts of the case disclosed a breach by the respondent State of its obligations under Article 6 para. 6-1. The applicants stated that they wished to take part in the proceedings and designated the lawyer who would represent them (Rule 30) The case concerns expropriation proceedings instituted with a view to the construction in the province of Vorarlberg of a provincial highway, the L 52. The proposed route was published (zur öffentlichen Einsichtnahme aufgelegt) and the file made available for consultation at the Rankweil council offices from 1 to 31 October 1984. It appears that the scheme in question dated back to 1960, but that opposition from local landowners had prevented its realisation. The authorities conducted an investigation into inter alia whether the projected road was compatible with the requirements of environmental protection (Landschaftsschutz). The Court heard addresses by them and also their replies to its questions. On 28 February 1985 expropriation proceedings relating to a parcel of land of 2,140m2 belonging to the Zumtobel partnership were opened. The authorities consulted several experts. According to the highways expert and the road traffic expert, the proposed section of highway was important because it would improve traffic links between Rankweil and Feldkirch, which went through densely populated built-up areas. The first applicant repeatedly but unsuccessfully requested to be allowed to study various documents in the file, namely a report of the Court of Audit (Rechnungshof), an expert report on the environmental implications, and an opinion of the environmental department of the Provincial Government. At the same time it dismissed two requests by the first applicant for full details of the planning procedure for the L 52. The Administrative Court dismissed the appeal on 22 September 1989, after a purely written procedure; the applicants had not asked it to hold a hearing. In the court’s opinion, the complaint that the scheme objected to was not based on any reasonable overall plan was not enough to establish that the contested decision had been unlawful. The court held that the applicant partnership had also failed to cast doubt on the official experts’ reports such as could disclose a procedural irregularity capable of affecting the road network. The Administrative Court cannot hold to be unlawful the fact that the respondent authority had regard to road traffic requirements and based its decision principally on the consideration that no other more appropriate solution was possible. The court considered that mere general remarks on the independence of official experts were not enough to prove a specific legitimate doubt. The fact that such an expert took part in proceedings to which the Province was a party did not, unless there were special circumstances, constitute a serious reason within the meaning of the 1950 Law to doubt his complete impartiality. The court stated that it could not find that the Office had disregarded procedural rules, compliance with which could have led to a different decision. As the applicant partnership had not been a party to the environmental protection proceedings (Landschaftsschutzverfahren), it couldn't claim a right to access the case file. There was nothing to show that these documents could have been material to the applicant partnership’s case or that the Office had based its decision on them. The Administrative Court also found that there had been no breach of Article 6 (art. 6) of the Convention and declined to refer the matter to the Constitutional Court. The first applicant had meanwhile applied to the Feldkirch District Court (Bezirksgericht) to determine the amount of compensation. On 17 December 1987 this was set at 9,963,032.50 Austrian schillings (ATS) The amount was reduced to ATS 4,560,000.50 on appeal (Rekurs) in 1988. The first applicant’s appeal on points of law (Revisionsrekurs) against this decision was dismissed by the Supreme Court (Oberster Gerichtshof) in October 1988. The appeal was dismissed on the grounds that it was not part of the original case. The case was appealed to the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), which dismissed the appeal in April 1989. The application was later dismissed on appeal on the basis that the decision was based on the ECHR's own decision. The ECHR ruled in favor of the applicant, and the case was dismissed in April 1990. The decision was upheld on appeal in October 1989.

Criminal proceedings were brought against the director of the Topkapı branch of the Bank and three other persons for having committed a fraud. On 9 July 1999 the Bakırköy Assize Court in Istanbul convicted the director and sentenced him to one year’s imprisonment for having abused his duty. The applicant appealed against this judgment arguing that the punishment imposed on the director was lenient. On 29 May 2001 the Court of Cassation quashed the above judgment. On 31 December 2004 the Bak Bakır Köy Assize Court terminated the criminal proceedings against the Director since they were time-barred.

The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. According to the Government, the total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. The appeal was based on several allegations of unlawfulness which, in their opinion, had tainted the procedure for informing the public about the proposed dam. They also claimed that the project breached the legislation on environmental protection, since no environmental impact study had been commissioned. In a judgment of 29 September 1995, the Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal.

The Spanish government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government filed their observations within 15 days of the hearing. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The court ruled that the law's constitutionality was not in breach of the Spanish Constitution, and that it was not a violation of the doctrine of non-interference in the affairs of the state. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's ruling was consistent with the law's enforcement by the Spanish government. The application was declared inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation which could be corrected. The court extended the question to include a new point raised by the applicant association, namely the constitutionality of section 18(3) (A.1.) and (B) of that law. The case was decided in favour of Navarre in 2000, and the Constitutional Court ruled that the law could continue to be enforced.

It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's. law was compatible with that of the Constitution, and that the law's enforcement was subject to the same rules as those in the constitution.

Within that Section, the Chamber that would consider the case (Article 27) would be the Court's Fourth Section. The case originated in an engineering project of February 1989 for the construction of a dam in Itoiz (Navarre province) which would result in the flooding of three nature reserves and a number of small villages. According to the Government, the total number of landowners affected by the dam's construction is 159. On 1 April 2003 the Chamber decided, having regard to the circumstances of the case, to dismiss a Rule 39 request submitted by the applicants. The applicants and the Government each filed observations on the merits (Rule 59 § 1). The application was declared admissible and reserved its position on the Government's preliminary questions as to whether the first five applicants lacked ‘victim’ status and had failed to exhaust domestic remedies. The Audiencia Nacional partly upheld the appeal, considering in particular that, according to the law, the planned dam should have been based on the national hydrological plan, which had not been drawn up when the project was approved. The court also accepted the request for precise designation of the protection zones around the nature reserves affected by the dam and for a breakdown of the quarry use that would be necessary for its construction. In 1996 the parliament of the Autonomous Community of Navarre (parlamento foral de Navarra) passed Autonomous community law (foral) no. 9/1996 on natural sites in Navarre. In application of the Autonomous Community law of 1996, the government of Navarre identified the peripheral protection zones for certain nature reserves and strict nature reserves in Navarre. According to the applicants, this Law enabled construction work on the dam to continue, with the consequent deterioration of the protected natural site. In a judgment of 14 July 1997, the Supreme Court definitively cancelled the dam project in so far as it concerned the 500-metre protection zones around nature reserves. The size of the planned dam, and thus of the area to be flooded, was reduced, so that the village of Itoiz, where the applicants' immovable property was located, was saved from flooding. The applicant association contested the authorities' argument, claiming that the Autonomous Community law of 1996 was inapplicable in the instant case. By a decision of 21 May 1998, the Constitutional Court declared the application inadmissible on account of certain errors in its presentation which could nonetheless be corrected. In the alternative, the applicant association requested that certain provisions in the Aut autonomous Community law be referred to the Constitutional court for a preliminary ruling on their constitutionality. Under section 37(2) of the Judicature Act, it gave notice of the questions to the Chamber of Deputies, the Senate, the government and parliament of Navarre and the Spanish government. The Constitutional Court, sitting as a full court, held that the impugned provisions of the Autonomous Community law of 1996 were compatible with the Constitution. It observed at the outset that enforcement of the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 had become impossible since the entry into force of the new law. The Constitutional Court also ruled that, given the significance of the question raised by the Itoiz dam's construction, which could not simply be ignored, it was justifiable that the explanatory memorandum accompanying the law specifically mentioned the aim and means of environmental protection in the peripheral protection zones around the three above-mentioned nature reserves. The Speaker of the Senate asked that the Senate be considered a party to the proceedings and offered its assistance. The Constitutional Court considered that a new law had been passed amending the legal system applicable to the peripheral protection zones and replacing the previous law on the basis of which the project had been declared partly void was not in itself incompatible with the right to execution of judicial decisions as enshrined in Article 24 of the Constitution. It found that both the Supreme Court's judgment of 14 July 1997 and the new Autonomous Community law of 1996 were intended to guarantee the existence of a peripheral protection zone around the three nature reserves affected by the dam's construction. The balance of general interests had been respected and that there was no clear lack of proportion between the conflicting interests. Outlined that laws could be challenged before the Constitutional Court through the remedy provided for in Article 163 of the Constitution. The Constitutional Court dismissed the application for a preliminary ruling. The judgment was published in the Official Gazette on 14 April 2000. It was published by the Government of South Africa in its Official Gazette. The decision was made by the Court of Appeal, which made the decision. The ruling was published as part of the Government’s appeal to the Supreme Court of the South African High Court. It said the decision was correct because it was based on the ruling of the High Court and not on a request from the applicant. The case was dismissed.

The applicant alleged that he did not have a fair trial as a result of the trial judge's misdirection to the jury on the drawing of adverse inferences as regards his refusal to answer questions during police interviews. The evidence against the applicant was almost entirely circumstantial and the case relied heavily on evidence from a police surveillance exercise carried out over a period of about one year. The Government were represented by their Agent, Ms J. Gladstone, of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office. The applicant pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to rob and other offences arising out of the conspiracy. He gave evidence in his own defence, claiming that he was not involved in the conspiracy or his associates' involvement. However, he admitted being involved in buying and selling stolen cars and argued that the police observations showed his involvement in that business, rather than in any conspiracy. The applicant also provided answers to all the questions which he had declined to answer during the police interviews in March and June 1997. The judge directed them as to the burden of proof and the standard of proof in the case: “...The burden [of proof] lies upon the prosecution throughout the case, to prove their case against the defendant. The defendant does not have to prove anything at all, there is no burden upon him to proveanything” The judge noted that the applicant had not answered questions put to him during the police interviews, replying ‘no comment’ to each of the questions posed. The judge also reminded the jury of some of the specific questions asked of the applicant during police interviews and of the subsequent answers relied upon by the applicant at trial. He concluded with the following direction: “If you think that the defendant has lied in evidence, but you think there is or might be some innocent explanation for any lie, then ignore it, take no notice of it at all.�” It is not of itself, evidence of guilt. A defendant may lie for many reasons. The applicant appealed to the Court of Appeal arguing that the summing up contained a Lucas direction (a direction to the jury in relation to lies – see paragraph 33) He was sentenced to 26 years' imprisonment. The trial judge described Mr Adetoro as a dangerous, cunning and intelligent man and he was satisfied that after he had joined the conspiracy, he had played a commanding role. The judge was not prepared to place reliance on anything he said and made no finding in respect of Mr Shearer and Mr Stephenson's presence or absence in the circumstances of the sixth robbery. He was a 'rather clever and determined liar' and his alibi 'fell apart' The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed. However, his sentence was reduced to 22 years' imprisonment. The Criminal Cases Review Commission (“CCRC”) referred the applicant's conviction to the Court of Appeal on the basis of the trial judge's direction to the jury. The main ground of appeal was that the direction on adverse inferences was defective in that the jury were not directed that an adverse inference could only be drawn where it was satisfied that the real reason for the applicant’s silence was that he had no answer to the questions asked, or no answer that would hold up to scrutiny. The Court of. Appeal disagreed and found that, despite the misdirection by the trialJudge, the conviction was safe. The court found that the jury had rejected the applicant's defence. It also noted that the judge had given the jury an unnecessary Lucas direction. The jury were told that if they thought there was an innocent explanation for any such lie told by the appellant they should not hold it against him. So, as the jury must have concluded that the appellant's explanation for his silence ('I wanted to protect others') was a lie, following the judge's direction they would have had to consider whether there was a innocent explanation before they could have used it as supportive of the Crown's case. If they did use his lying explanation against him, the jury would have concluded the lie was not innocent – in other words the reason he had no answer to them or none which would withstand scrutiny. The applicant's appeal against conviction was dismissed on 7 June 2006. The judge found the evidence against the applicant to be overwhelming. The jury could not decide whether to convict or acquit the applicant. The appeal was dismissed by the Court of Appeal. The case was settled at a later hearing in June 2006, and the applicant was cleared of all charges against him.
